The Blue-footed Booby (Sula nebouxii) is a long-lived seabird in which reproductive output is constrained by the demands of a single, slow-growing chick. Newly hatched nestlings emerge after an incubation period of approximately 41 days [ab = approximately 41 days] when eggs are maintained at a typical adult body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], though this thermal target can vary considerably under natural conditions. At hatching, the altricial chick weighs a modest 46 grams [Wwb = 46 grams], a relatively small mass that underscores the substantial parental investment required over the subsequent weeks. This initial wet weight is the starting point for a growth trajectory that culminates in an ultimate adult body mass of 1580 grams [Wwi = 1580 grams] once the bird reaches full size. The dramatic increase from hatchling to adult mass reflects the rich marine food resources available in the booby's upwelling-driven foraging habitat, as well as the intense biparental provisioning that characterizes the species' breeding system.

Using data from related Sulidae species, particularly the red-footed booby (Sula sula), researchers have estimated several key developmental milestones under the warm-body conditions typical of active adult boobies. At an internal temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging — when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and becomes capable of leaving the nest — has been reported around 100 days after hatching [tx = around 100 days after hatching]. This relatively extended pre-fledging period is consistent with the altricial development pattern of the Sulidae and allows for the full growth of flight feathers and the accumulation of substantial fat reserves. Fledging represents a critical transition, as the juvenile must then navigate the challenging learning curve of plunge-diving to capture prey independently.

Following the fledging milestone, the immature bird enters a prolonged juvenile phase that eventually culminates in sexual maturation. Data derived from the closely related Sula sula indicate that the time since birth at puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development, is approximately 300 days after hatching [tp = approximately 300 days after hatching] at the typical active body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This value places the onset of reproductive capability within the first year of life, a timeline that is comparatively rapid among long-lived seabirds. The attainment of puberty does not immediately lead to breeding, however, as social structure, territory acquisition, and experience often defer actual nesting attempts.

First reproduction in the Blue-footed Booby occurs later than the initial attainment of sexual maturity, a pattern common among colonially nesting seabirds where competition for mates and nest sites is intense. Using life-history data from Sula sula as a comparative benchmark, the time since birth at first brood is estimated at approximately 2.5 years [tR = approximately 2.5 years] when measured at the standard body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This delay between puberty and first successful reproduction reflects the need for young birds to acquire sufficient foraging proficiency and to establish a breeding territory. The species is capable of only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], and within that clutch females typically produce one to two eggs [N_R_i = clutch females typically produce one to two eggs].

Longevity records for the Blue-footed Booby indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years], a value consistent with the slow life-history pace of many tropical and subtropical seabirds when maintained at a core body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This extended lifespan allows individuals numerous breeding seasons to compensate for the low annual reproductive output inherent in the species. Senescence in this species is marked by a gradual decline in foraging efficiency and chick-provisioning capacity, with the oldest breeding adults often showing reduced fledging success. The combination of a maximum reproductive rate of roughly 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = roughly 1 clutch per year], each containing 1 to 2 eggs [N_R_i = each containing 1 to 2 eggs], and a long adult lifespan aligns with bet-hedging life-history strategies typical of colonial seabirds that face high annual variability in marine prey availability.
